findings.title: tempfile.mkstemp sits outside the try, so a config-dir OSError becomes an unhandled 500
findings.problem: `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` runs before the `try:`. The docstring (D-17) says file-write failure is non-fatal and that OSError is never re-raised. mkstemp can raise OSError in several cases: the config directory is read-only (for example a read-only Docker volume mount), it is out of space or inodes, or it has the wrong ownership. That error leaves `_write_reset_token_file`, passes through `run_in_executor`, and propagates out of `reset_request_post` at routes.py:1698 with no handler. By then the token is already minted into app.state and written to the log, so the user gets a 500 instead of the neutral confirmation, and the failure skips the sanitized error log the function promises. A config dir that is not writable is the scenario this non-fatal path was designed for.
findings.fix_hint: move mkstemp inside the try (initialise tmp_path=None and skip the unlink when it is None), or wrap it in its own OSError handler that logs and returns
findings.why_it_matters: The recovery endpoint returns a server error in exactly the read-only or full-disk deployments where the file sink fails, which contradicts the documented D-17 guarantee.

findings.title: Raw fd leaks if os.fchmod (or os.fdopen) raises before the file object owns it
findings.problem: mkstemp returns a raw OS fd. Only the `with os.fdopen(fd, ...)` block closes it. If `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` raises OSError (for example EPERM on some network or FUSE filesystems), or if os.fdopen itself fails, the except branch logs the error and unlinks tmp_path but never calls os.close(fd). The `finally` closes only dir_fd. The whole acquire-to-release scope is in this function.
findings.fix_hint: track whether fdopen took ownership and os.close(fd) in the except/finally when it did not
findings.why_it_matters: Each failed reset request leaks a file descriptor in a long-running daemon.

findings.title: Password reset token logged in cleartext and surfaced in the authenticated web UI log viewer
findings.problem: The freshly minted CSPRNG reset token is interpolated directly into a `logger.warning(...)` call. I verified in triggarr/startup.py `collect_secrets()` (lines ~95-100) that the redacting sink only ever redacts `password_hash`, `api_key`, and `session_secret` — the reset token is never added to that list, exactly as the code's own comment states ('intentionally NOT added to collect_secrets'). I also traced the downstream path in triggarr/logging.py: `setup_logging()`'s `buffer_sink` redacts using that same `secrets` list and then stores the unredacted token text in the in-memory `log_buffer` (triggarr/log_buffer.py, maxlen=200). That buffer is read by the existing `/` dashboard route and the `/partials/log-viewer` htmx endpoint (triggarr/web/routes.py:382, :1083) and rendered verbatim as `{{ entry.message }}` in triggarr/templates/partials/log_viewer.html:67/80, which auto-refreshes every 5 seconds. So the token does not just land in `docker logs` (the intended 'operator-only' channel) — it is also returned in an authenticated HTTP response body.
findings.current_code:
logger.warning(
    "Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}",
    token=token,
)
findings.fix_hint: Do not log the raw token value; log only that a token was minted (optionally with a short, non-sensitive prefix) and rely solely on the 0600 reset-token.txt file as the operator recovery channel, or add the token to the `secrets` list passed to `setup_logging`/`collect_secrets` right before logging it and remove it immediately after (so it is redacted from both the stderr sink and the in-memory UI log buffer) while still writing the full value to the file.
findings.why_it_matters: This token is a bearer credential that can be redeemed to reset the operator's password (full account takeover). The new code's own comments assert an explicit invariant — 'The token NEVER appears in any HTTP response body, header, or template context' — but that invariant is false: because the token bypasses the existing redaction allowlist, it flows into the same in-memory log buffer that feeds the dashboard's live log viewer, so any party with an authenticated session (cookie, X-Api-Key, or Basic auth — all equally privileged in AuthMiddleware) can read the token straight out of the web UI within ~30 log lines of the mint, with no need for host/docker access at all. It also conflicts with the project's own absolute rule to never log sensitive tokens.

members.title: Reset token value deliberately written to logs
members.problem: Global CLAUDE.md, under the absolute Security section, states: "Never log sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII, auth headers)." This code calls `logger.warning("Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}", token=token)`, deliberately interpolating the live password-reset token value into a log line. The code comments (D-02 + RESEARCH #4) frame this as an intentional 'operator-only' recovery channel and explicitly exclude the token from the app's own redacting sink, but the written rule carries no such carve-out and is marked absolute ('Precedence: the Security rules below are absolute').

findings.title: tempfile.mkstemp() call sits outside the try/except that is documented as this function's error boundary
findings.problem: Global CLAUDE.md states: "Add try/except around external calls (DB, HTTP, file I/O) only where this code is the intended error boundary." This function's own docstring and inline comments declare it IS that boundary for the reset-token file write ("D-17: in-memory token is the authority; file write failure is non-fatal... Do NOT re-raise"), but `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` executes before the `try:` block, so an OSError from mkstemp itself (e.g. missing/unwritable config dir) is not caught here and propagates uncaught to the `run_in_executor` await in `reset_request_post`, which also has no try/except around it.
findings.current_code:
dir_fd = None
    renamed = False
    fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")
    try:
        os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)
findings.fix_hint: Move the mkstemp call inside the try block (or wrap it separately) so its OSError is caught by the same non-fatal handling as the rest of the write path.
findings.why_it_matters: If the config directory is missing or not writable on first run, this breaks the documented D-17 guarantee that a reset-token file-write failure is non-fatal: the exception surfaces in the request handler instead of being logged and swallowed, turning what should be a silent degrade (token still usable from the log) into an unhandled-exception path.

members.title: An error creating the temp file escapes the non-fatal handler, so /reset/request returns 500 after the token is already minted
members.problem: `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` runs before the `try:` block, so the `except OSError` handler does not cover it. Triggers: a read-only config volume, ENOSPC, EACCES, or a config dir whose ownership does not match the container UID. In any of these cases mkstemp raises OSError inside `run_in_executor`, the exception propagates from `await ... run_in_executor(...)` at routes.py:1698, and the client gets a 500 instead of the neutral confirmation. By that point the in-memory token has been set (line 1680), the token has been logged (line 1689) and the 60s rate-limit stamp has been written (line 1656). Recovery still works through docker logs, but the docstring promises file-write failure is non-fatal (D-17), and an unhandled 500 may expose framework error details depending on the exception handlers. The same pattern exists in config.py:110 and state.py:203, but this is the only site that claims a never-raises guarantee.

findings.title: Raw fd from mkstemp leaks if fchmod (or anything before os.fdopen) raises
findings.problem: `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(...)` returns a raw OS-level file descriptor that is only handed to a context manager at `with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:` (line 1578). If `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` on line 1577 raises OSError, execution jumps straight to the `except OSError` handler, which unlinks `tmp_path` but never closes the bare `fd` — it is leaked for the life of the process since nothing else references or finalizes a raw int fd.
findings.fix_hint: wrap the fchmod call inside `with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:` (fchmod on f.fileno()) so the fd is owned by the context manager from the first line that can fail, or add an explicit `os.close(fd)` in the except branch guarded by a flag tracking whether fdopen has already taken ownership
findings.why_it_matters: This is a long-running daemon (per CLAUDE.md, triggarr is a Python automation daemon); repeated fd leaks on this error path (e.g. a transient permission/SELinux/filesystem quirk preventing fchmod) will eventually exhaust the process's file descriptor limit, causing unrelated failures elsewhere in the app.

# is already 0600 after os.replace with no post-rename chmod window.

members.title: Raw fd from mkstemp not closed if os.fchmod() raises before fdopen
members.problem: Global CLAUDE.md states: "Ensure resources are released on every path... try/finally for everything else." `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` runs on the raw fd returned by `tempfile.mkstemp` before `os.fdopen(fd, "w")` wraps it in a context manager. If `os.fchmod` itself raises OSError, the except branch unlinks `tmp_path` but never closes the bare integer `fd`, and the `finally` only closes `dir_fd` (never assigned in this path) — the file descriptor leaks.

members.why_it_matters: This is a rare-trigger (fchmod must fail) but real fd leak; repeated failures (e.g. a persistently misconfigured volume) would exhaust the process's file descriptor table over time.
members.fix_hint: Wrap `fd` in `os.fdopen` (or a try/finally closing `fd`) before calling `os.fchmod`, or fchmod via the file object after fdopen so the context manager always owns the descriptor.

findings.title: The exposed reset flow has no token-consumption endpoint
findings.problem: GET /reset/request now exposes a password-recovery form and POST mints a token, but the registered router contains no /reset/confirm handler or other reset-token consumer. The existing confirmation form targets /reset/confirm (templates/reset.html:29), which returns 404. Thus an operator can request and retrieve a token but cannot use it to recover access; the newly activated flow requires the missing consumer.
